summary: Eight coverage gaps (1 critical, 6 major, 1 minor) plus two bloat findings. The largest is that the corpus's one independent, published, benchmarked precedent for the exact recommended architecture (RAMSES, arXiv 2511.21413 — external-registry-fed discovery bridging a Kubernetes gateway to Slurm-launched vLLM) is cited nowhere in the draft, while the draft repeatedly concedes 'no precedent'. Secondary gaps cluster around llm-d components the inventory table silently drops (Coordinator, Inference Payload Processor, the pluggable KV-index backend) and around downstream-consumer reuse precedent (KServe LLMInferenceService, KAITO).

findings.location: Section 6D ('Steel-manning the strongest objection') and Section 7B Phase 3 / Section 8 ('The extension pattern is sound but unratified')
findings.issue: The corpus contains a peer-reviewed, benchmarked production precedent for precisely the architecture the report recommends — a gateway that enumerates vLLM endpoints from an external registry instead of from Kubernetes Pod objects, with a bridge process reconciling that registry against Slurm job state — and the draft never cites it. The draft instead asserts 'no precedent' three separate times (Section 3C: 'you would become the first person ever...'; Section 4C's audited absence; Section 8's 'no known importers'). Those concessions are correct about out-of-tree Go registration against llm-d specifically, but as written they read as though the *pattern* is unprecedented. In an advocate-register report defending the discovery-seam thesis, leaving the one independent validation of that pattern on the floor is a self-inflicted weakening of the thesis and of the steel-man's rebuttal.
findings.evidence: [[automated-dynamic-ai-inference-scaling-on]] (arXiv:2511.21413, MIND '25, RAMSES supercomputer, Ruhr Univ. Bochum / Univ. of Cologne): a Kubernetes-hosted OpenAI-compatible 'Web Gateway' 'looks up available vLLM endpoints from a central PostgreSQL table (ai_model_endpoints) rather than from Kubernetes Pod objects'; a long-running 'Job Worker' background process is 'the sole component that talks to Slurm', reconciling endpoint-job rows against model configurations and submitting/removing vLLM-serving Slurm jobs; Apptainer as the HPC container runtime. Reported benchmark: scales to 100/500/1000 concurrent requests with roughly 500 ms added end-to-end latency versus direct vLLM access. The coverage-gaps file lists this note as load-bearing for Q5 and Q7 and names it explicitly under gap resolution #2 ('Independent precedent outside llm-d: RAMSES Postgres-fed discovery'). Note is entirely uncited in the draft. Adjacent uncited support: [[a-system-for-microserving-of-llms]] (arXiv:2412.12488, MLSys) — a programmable router whose dispatch logic is written against an abstract list of engine objects rather than orchestrator objects.
findings.recommendation: Add two-to-three sentences in Section 6D, after the sentence beginning 'Every clause of that is true...', introducing RAMSES as an independent precedent: the generator-plus-registry rung is not a theory, it is a published production HPC deployment whose measured overhead at up to 1000 concurrent requests is about 500 ms end to end. Then add a qualifying clause to the 'no precedent' concessions in Section 3C and Section 8 so they are scoped precisely: what is unprecedented is out-of-tree registration against llm-d's Go registry, not external-registry-fed discovery for Slurm-class estates, which has an independent published implementation. Note explicitly that RAMSES is a bespoke gateway, not built on llm-d/GIE, so it validates the pattern and not the code path — otherwise the patch overclaims.

findings.location: Section 1B (the component inventory table) and Section 5E ('The one functional loss')
findings.issue: The inventory table presents itself as the answer to the query's first clause ('use llm-d components as much as possible'), but it omits two shipped llm-d-router components that the corpus documents and that have distinct Kubernetes-coupling profiles. (a) The **Coordinator** — a Go service in the same repository that drives requests through a configurable pipeline of steps (download media, tokenize, encode, prefill, decode) and is a third plugin seam in its own right. (b) The **Inference Payload Processor (IPP)**, llm-d v0.9's multi-model routing component, successor to Body-Based Routing. IPP's omission also leaves Section 5E's strong claim ('Per-request priority via InferenceObjective is the single genuine gap') under-defended: a reader with a multi-model estate needs to know that IPP's body-to-header extraction is portable but its downstream steering is not, because it 'lets HTTPRoutes direct traffic to the appropriate InferencePool' and off-cluster there are no HTTPRoutes or pools to steer into.
findings.evidence: [[llm-d-routerdocscoordinator_architecturemd-at-main-llm-dllm-d-router-github]] (uncited): 'The coordinator is a Go service that accepts inference requests and drives them through a configurable pipeline of steps... The pre-processing steps call side services directly (media download, and the render service for tokenization); the encode, prefill, and decode steps forward sub-requests to vLLM worker pools through an Inference Gateway that conforms to GAIE. An Endpoint Picker (EPP) behind the gateway selects the concrete pod for each phase, so the coordinator orchestrates the phases without knowing pod addresses.' Also: 'The coordinator is stateless... Any instance can serve any request, so the service scales horizontally by running more replicas behind a load balancer with no coordination between them' and 'steps are self-contained plugins registered by name'. Companion note [[llm-d-routerdocscoordinator_async_brokermd-at-main-llm-dllm-d-router-github]] (uncited). IPP: [[llm-d-v09-hardened-for-scale-llm-d]] — 'Multi-model routing introduces the Inference Payload Processor (IPP), enabling multiple LLMs to serve behind a single gateway endpoint. IPP extracts the model name from request bodies and sets routing headers, letting HTTPRoutes direct traffic to the appropriate InferencePool.' Corroborated by [[monitor-llm-routing-with-the-kubernetes-inference-extension-datadog]] on the BBR predecessor and by [[gateway-api-inference-extension-with-llm-d-router-kaito]] ('Optional Body-Based Routing (BBR) that extracts model names from OpenAI-style requests and injects a header'). The run's own interim report [[interim-report-lost-k8s-policy-inputs]] adjudicates IPP as a read path, not a canary-decision write path — and flags that the IPP repo itself was escalation-blocked, so the treatment must stay at blog-level fidelity.
findings.recommendation: Add two rows to the Section 1B table. Coordinator: 'Drives a request through a step pipeline (media download, tokenize, encode, prefill, decode); stateless, step plugins registered by name' / coupling 'None in the coordinator itself — it forwards sub-requests through a GAIE-conformant gateway and never learns pod addresses' / 'Yes, but new (docs landed 2026-09-10) and it presumes a gateway+EPP in front of the pools'. IPP: 'Extracts model name from the request body and sets a routing header for multi-model fan-out' / coupling 'The header is consumed by HTTPRoutes selecting an InferencePool' / 'Body-parsing half travels; the HTTPRoute steering half does not — map the header to a pool in your own Envoy route config, or run one picker per pool.' Then add one sentence to Section 5E noting that multi-model fan-out is the second policy input whose Kubernetes half does not travel, and that the substitute is an Envoy header-match route rather than an HTTPRoute. Keep the IPP claim at blog-level fidelity and say so — the repo could not be fetched.

findings.location: Section 7A Rule 1 (Active-Active branch, the paragraph beginning 'That last branch needs its evidence stated') and Section 5C
findings.issue: The report's multi-replica off-Kubernetes recommendation rests entirely on the argument that each router replica converges independently because the precise extractor does not implement the cross-replica syncer, with the syncer itself dismissed as future work. That is accurate but incomplete: llm-d's own KV-cache indexer ships a **pluggable index backend** with a shipped external (Valkey/Redis, optionally RDMA) implementation that lets replicas share one KV block index rather than each rebuilding its own. For a query whose first clause is 'use llm-d components as much as possible', a shipped llm-d component that directly addresses the report's hardest topology problem — and that is configured by an environment variable, with no Kubernetes dependency whatsoever — is a material omission. It also bears on the restart-recovery discussion in Section 5C, where the draft's only answer is vLLM's 5559 replay socket.
findings.evidence: [[llm-d-kv-cachedocsarchitecturemd-at-main-llm-dllm-d-kv-cache-github]] (uncited): module table lists 'kvblock.Index — The block index itself. Pluggable interface storing requestKey → []PodEntry plus the auxiliary engineKey → requestKey map. Default Implementation: Two-level in-memory LRU.' Also: 'The library is designed to be embedded in a host process (llm-d's EPP is the reference consumer); it is not a standalone service' and 'New integrations tokenize externally and call ScoreTokens directly.' [[llm-d-kv-cacheexamplesvalkey_examplereadmemd-at-v040-llm-dllm-d-kv-cache-github]] (uncited): 'demonstrates how to use Valkey as the backend for the KV-Cache Manager's KV-block indexing system'; configuration is VALKEY_ADDR / VALKEY_ENABLE_RDMA environment variables; 'Multi-Pod Lookup: demonstrates cache sharing across multiple pods'; landed via 'feat: Add Valkey and RDMA support for KV-cache indexing (#139)'. The draft cites the sibling configuration doc [[llm-d-kv-cachedocsconfigurationmd-at-main-llm-dllm-d-kv-cache-github]] once for static endpoint mode, so the repository is already in scope.
findings.recommendation: Add two or three sentences to the Active-Active paragraph in Section 7A Rule 1, after the sentence explaining that each replica converges independently: state that the index backend is itself pluggable and that a shared Valkey backend is shipped and configured purely by environment variable, so a team unwilling to rely on independent convergence has an llm-d-native shared-index option that costs an external datastore rather than a peer-discovery plugin. Flag honestly that the example is an example, not a documented production topology, and that it adds a datastore to the failure domain — do not upgrade it to a recommendation. Optionally add a half-sentence to Section 5C noting a shared index is a second answer to post-restart index recovery alongside the replay socket.

findings.location: Section 6D (asset list), Section 8 final paragraph ('The trade-off you are actually making'), and the Section 1B inventory row for the latency predictor
findings.issue: Predicted-latency scoring is sold twice as part of 'llm-d's plugin depth — the asset you are buying', and the inventory table marks the latency predictor reusable off-pod with no qualification ('Plain HTTP services on fixed ports, no API-server dependency'). The corpus carries a documented disqualifier that lands hardest on exactly the estates this report targets: the predictor assumes a single pod shape and is explicitly not a fit for heterogeneous pools. Bare-metal racks assembled over time, Slurm partitions with mixed accelerators, and serverless GPU providers are heterogeneous by default. The corpus also documents that the predictor is deployed as sidecar containers colocated with the EPP — a pod-spec construct with no off-Kubernetes equivalent, so the operator must colocate and supervise two extra processes themselves. Under the advocate register, selling an asset the reader may be unable to use, without the caveat the vendor itself publishes, is a commitment-quality defect rather than a mere omission.
findings.evidence: [[predicted-latency-based-scheduling-llm-d]] (uncited): 'Predicted latency is not a fit when the pool is heterogeneous — mixed GPU types, model variants (e.g. prefill vs decode), or serving configurations in the same pool will produce inaccurate predictions, because the predictor assumes a single pod shape.' Same note: 'The setup deploys an EPP with the predicted latency sidecar containers: Training Server — trains the XGBoost model to predict TPOT and TTFT based on observed traffic; Prediction Servers — predict TPOT and TTFT of the request based on current server state', and the request flow requires the proxy to send results back to the training server. Companion guide note [[llm-dguidespredicted-latency-routing-at-main-llm-dllm-d-github]] also uncited. The draft currently cites only [[github-llm-dllm-d-latency-predictor-latency-prediction-service-for-ml-model-base]] for this component.
findings.recommendation: Qualify in place rather than adding a section. In the Section 1B inventory row, append to the coupling cell that the reference deployment colocates training and prediction servers as EPP sidecars, which off-Kubernetes becomes your own process-supervision job. Then add one sentence immediately after the asset list in Section 6D: predicted-latency scoring is conditional on a homogeneous pool — upstream documents it as inapplicable to mixed GPU types, model variants, or serving configurations — so estates with heterogeneous hardware should discount that line item from the value they are buying. One clause in the Section 8 closing list is enough to keep the two mentions consistent.

findings.location: Section 3C ('Registration, and the objection it invites'), in the 'answer, in three moves' passage
findings.issue: The draft's precedent objection is stated at full strength and then answered on three grounds, none of which is the strongest available: two significant downstream projects already consume the llm-d Router EPP as a component, unmodified, as their endpoint picker. That is direct evidence for the query's actual premise ('use llm-d components as much as possible') and it sharpens rather than blurs the real concession — component reuse of the router is well precedented; out-of-tree Go plugin registration is not. As drafted, the reader cannot distinguish those two, and the report looks more isolated than it is. The corpus is unambiguous that these consumers are all Kubernetes-based, which is precisely why the distinction needs stating rather than hiding.
findings.evidence: [[gateway-api-inference-extension-with-llm-d-router-kaito]] (uncited): 'In KAITO, the EPP is provided by the llm-d Router project, which builds on the GWIE EPP with advanced scheduling plugins including KV cache-aware routing, prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregation, and pluggable filters/scorers'; enabled by a single feature gate from KAITO v0.8.0, default-on from v0.11.0. [[announcing-kserve-v017-production-ready-llm-serving-with-llminferenceservice-kse]] (uncited): KServe v0.17 'brings LLMInferenceService to production readiness with a GenAI-first architecture built on the llm-d framework', creating 'the Deployment, Service, Gateway, HTTPRoute, InferencePool, InferenceModel, and EPP (Endpoint Picker Pod) — all managed by the LLMInferenceService controller'. Also [[best-of-both-worlds-cloud-native-ai-inference-at-scale-using-kserve-and-llm-d-ks]], which the draft cites once for an unrelated benchmark caveat. Coverage-gaps lists KServe v0.17 and KAITO as load-bearing sources for Q1 — they are effectively unused.
findings.recommendation: Insert two sentences into Section 3C's 'answer' passage, before or after the 'fork dodges none of it' move: name KAITO and KServe v0.17 as projects that consume the llm-d Router EPP as their endpoint picker without modifying it, then immediately state the limit — both do so on Kubernetes, through the published chart and image, so they establish that the EPP is treated as a reusable component and establish nothing about out-of-tree registration. Keep the isolation concession intact; the point is to bound it, not to dissolve it.

findings.location: Section 6B ('Dispatching the shims') and the strategy-table row F in Section 6A
findings.issue: Section 6B dispatches exactly two shims — hand-authored EndpointSlices and virtual-kubelet. The corpus identifies a third that the draft never names: InferencePoolImport, the one documented mechanism by which InferencePool-adjacent routing reaches endpoints outside the local cluster's Pod set. Any reader who researches 'can InferencePool point at something that is not a local pod?' will find it, and the report's category-error argument ('pool membership lists pods by label selector') reads as incomplete until it is dispatched. This matters more than the other shims because it does not fail on the same grounds: it is controller-managed rather than user-authored, and in its only shipping form it is vendor-proprietary plumbing over real pools in real clusters. It also connects to the 'Remote Kubernetes clusters' row already in the Section 5B table, giving the reader the choice between llm-d's multicluster-file-discovery plugin and the gateway-tier import CRD.
findings.evidence: [[api-overview-kubernetes-gateway-api-inference-extension]] (uncited): InferencePool 'is explicitly positioned as a drop-in replacement for a Kubernetes Service', and InferencePoolImport is 'a cluster-local, CONTROLLER-managed (not user-authored) representation of an InferencePool imported from another cluster, populated by a multi-cluster controller, allowing traffic to be routed to model servers running in a remote cluster — this is the one documented mechanism by which InferencePool-adjacent routing can reach endpoints outside the local cluster's Pod set'. [[multi-cluster-gke-inference-gateway-helps-scale-ai-workloads-google-cloud-blog]] (uncited): the exported pool 'surfaces in the config cluster as a new, GCP-proprietary GCPInferencePoolImport resource, to which a GCPBackendPolicy attaches for cross-cluster load-balancing signals'; the note's own assessment is that 'InferencePool itself still only ever groups Pods within a single cluster; cross-cluster reach is solved by a new import CRD + GCP control plane, not by relaxing what InferencePool can select.' The run's interim report [[interim-report-topology-and-k8s-shims]] flagged this as an unchased follow-up.
findings.recommendation: Add three sentences to Section 6B, between the EndpointSlice paragraph and the virtual-kubelet paragraph: name InferencePoolImport, state precisely what it is (controller-populated, not user-authored; a representation of a real pool in a real remote cluster), and dispatch it — it relaxes where the pods live, not what a pool can select, and its only shipping implementation is GCP-proprietary. Close by pointing the cross-cluster reader at the multicluster-file-discovery row already in the Section 5B table. No new section needed.

findings.location: Section 5E ('The one functional loss') and Section 8 ('The custom surface tends to grow')
findings.issue: The report contains no treatment of autoscaling at all — zero mentions across roughly 9,600 words — while committing to the strong claim that per-request priority is 'the single genuine gap'. The corpus documents that llm-d v0.9 made the router the source of truth for pool scaling signals and migrated the actuation path to KEDA, a Kubernetes-only component, with the Workload Variant Autoscaler on the legacy Prometheus Adapter path. Off Kubernetes the signals survive on the EPP's metrics endpoint but nothing consumes them, so pool elasticity joins InferenceObjective as a capability whose Kubernetes half does not travel. This also interacts with advice the report already gives: saturation-gated admission and the flow-control queue behave differently against a fleet that cannot grow, and the Section 5B row for serverless GPU providers already gestures at cold starts without connecting them to who decides to scale.
findings.evidence: [[llm-d-v09-hardened-for-scale-llm-d]] (cited in the draft only for the model-server-interface roadmap line): 'KEDA begins replacing Prometheus Adapter as the autoscaling foundation'; 'New guides land for KEDA + EPP pool-level saturation metrics, where the endpoint picker exposes queue depth, in-flight request counts, and KV-cache pressure as KEDA-compatible scaling signals. The router becomes the source of truth for scaling decisions rather than relying on Prometheus queries against model server metrics. SLO-driven autoscaling combines KEDA with the predicted latency scorer'; 'The Workload Variant Autoscaler continues to support the existing Prometheus Adapter path'. Corroborating framing in [[serving-pytorch-llms-at-scale-disaggregated]] (uncited), which describes llm-d as an 'LLM aware inference gateway + LLM aware autoscaler'. Datadog's account of central-queue flow control notes it 'enables scale-to-zero for batch workloads since requests queue centrally while GPU pods spin up' [[monitor-llm-routing-with-the-kubernetes-inference-extension-datadog]] (uncited) — the scale-up half of that is precisely what does not travel.
findings.recommendation: Amend the opening commitment of Section 5E so it is defensible: per-request priority is the single loss on the *request path*, and pool autoscaling is the loss on the *capacity path*. Add two sentences: the EPP still exposes queue depth, in-flight counts and KV-cache pressure as scaling signals off-cluster, but KEDA and the Workload Variant Autoscaler are the Kubernetes-side consumers, so an off-cluster operator supplies their own actuator against the same metrics. One clause in Section 8's 'custom surface tends to grow' listing the actuator as a non-Go work item keeps the accounting honest.

findings.location: Section 5B (the managed-API row commentary) and Section 5A (observability sentence) / Section 7B Phase 0
findings.issue: Two recommendations are argued entirely from third-party sources when llm-d's own v0.9 material supports them directly, and one operational trap for version-pinning is missing. (a) The two-tier gateway pattern for managed providers is defended with an AKS engineering blog and a Red Hat article; llm-d itself ships integration guides for fronting llm-d with LiteLLM and Kong AI Gateway for exactly that purpose, and the Gateway API Inference Extension's own API overview names LiteLLM, Gloo AI Gateway and Apigee as the layer where self-hosted models sit alongside model-as-a-service providers. (b) The observability treatment names no metric the reader should actually scrape or alert on, and omits that v0.9 renamed the EPP KV metrics into the llm_d_router_epp subsystem — directly relevant to a report whose Phase 0 instructs pinning a tagged release and whose floor is v0.9.0.
findings.evidence: [[llm-d-v09-hardened-for-scale-llm-d]]: 'LiteLLM and Kong AI Gateway integration guides land for operators who want to front llm-d with an API management layer that handles authentication, rate limiting, and model routing across multiple providers'; and 'The metric renames in this release (EPP KV metrics move to the llm_d_router_epp subsystem) require dashboard and alert updates — deprecated aliases are available during the transition.' [[api-overview-kubernetes-gateway-api-inference-extension]] (uncited): the extension 'makes it easy to expose and control access to your local OpenAI-compatible chat completion endpoints to other workloads on or off cluster, or to integrate your self-hosted models alongside model-as-a-service providers in a higher level AI Gateways like LiteLLM, Gloo AI Gateway, or Apigee.' [[monitor-llm-routing-with-the-kubernetes-inference-extension-datadog]] (uncited) supplies concrete metric names — inference_objective_request_duration_seconds, inference_pool_per_pod_queue_size, inference_extension_flow_control_request_queue_duration_seconds labelled by outcome=Rejected/Evicted — and is itself third-party precedent for monitoring the EPP without cluster-native tooling.
findings.recommendation: Add one clause to the managed-API commentary in Section 5B citing llm-d's own LiteLLM and Kong integration guides, so the 'keep the pool homogeneous' verdict is llm-d-endorsed rather than inferred from competitors. Add one sentence to the Section 5A observability passage naming the two or three metrics worth alerting on off-cluster (per-pod queue size, flow-control queue duration by outcome, request duration) and noting that the v0.9 EPP KV metric rename to the llm_d_router_epp subsystem means dashboards must match the pinned version.

findings.issue: Bloat. The report runs roughly 9,600 words / 73 KB against a 45-55 KB reference norm, and the excess is concentrated in a tail that restates settled conclusions rather than adding evidence. Section 8 carries five successive concluding passages — 'Falsification conditions', 'Forward look', 'The compounding implication for design', 'What is not recommended', and 'The trade-off you are actually making' — of which three make the same point (keep the custom surface to one plugin; the plugin is the only churn-exposed artifact; the exchange is favourable if you use the scheduling stack). Section 7C 'Standing obligations' immediately precedes them and re-lists commitments already stated as Rules 1-4 on the previous page: health-gated upsert/delete (Rule 3), pinned release plus CI (Rule 2 escalation and Phase 3), proxy failure mode (Rule 4), sidecar isolation plus prefill TLS (Section 5D and Phase 4). 'What is not recommended' re-verdicts strategies D, E, F and the managed-API row already decided in Section 6A's table.
findings.evidence: Verbatim repetition of the value proposition: line 229 'precise prefix-cache routing, load and queue awareness, saturation-gated admission, priority and fairness queuing, disaggregation profile handling, predicted-latency scoring' and line 304 'precise prefix affinity, load and queue awareness, saturation-gated admission, priority and fairness queuing, disaggregation profiles, predicted-latency scoring'. 'Keep the custom surface to one plugin' recurs at lines 239, 280, 288 and 300. Section 7C's four commitments each map one-to-one onto a Rule stated in Section 7A.
findings.recommendation: Cut Section 7C down to a single sentence that points back at Rules 1-4 and keeps only the genuinely new content (the organisational fifth commitment: one plugin, named owner). Merge 'The compounding implication for design' into the preceding forward-look paragraph as one clause. Delete 'What is not recommended' outright — every item in it is a verdict already delivered in the Section 6A table with reasoning attached — or reduce it to a single line. That is roughly 400-500 words removed with no evidence lost, which also creates room for the coverage patches above without growing the report.

findings.location: Lead paragraph and Section 8 final paragraph ('The trade-off you are actually making')
findings.issue: The opening paragraph and the closing paragraph make the same argument with overlapping phrasing: customize exactly one seam, reuse everything above it, the scheduling stack survives, the plugin is the only thing you would rewrite. The closing paragraph's one genuinely distinct contribution — the negative case, that a workload with no shared prefixes, no disaggregation and no multi-tenant contention should choose a simpler router — is buried mid-paragraph behind the restatement.
findings.recommendation: Differentiate the close rather than deleting it. Lead with the negative case ('If your workload has no shared prefixes...') as the first clause of the final paragraph, drop the restatement of the one-seam thesis, and end on something the lead cannot contain because it depends on Section 8's findings — the two named commits (a documented out-of-tree posture; a pluggable coordination primitive) that would change the calculus, and the fact that the reversibility of the bet, not its expected value, is what justifies starting now.
